subject.title: The War-song of Dinas Vawr
subject.author: Thomas Love Peacock
subject.text:
The mountain sheep are sweeter,
But the valley sheep are fatter;
We therefore deemed it meeter
To carry off the latter.
We made an expedition;
We met a host, and quelled it;
We forced a strong position,
And killed the men who held it.

On Dyfed's richest valley,
Where herds of kine were browsing,
We made a mighty sally,
To furnish our carousing.
Fierce warriors rushed to meet us;
We met them, and o'erthrew them:
They struggled hard to beat us;
But we conquered them, and slew them.

As we drove our prize at leisure,
The king marched forth to catch us:
His rage surpassed all measure,
But his people could not match us.
He fled to his hall-pillars;
And, ere our force we led off,
Some sacked his house and cellars,
While others cut his head off.

We there, in strife bewild'ring,
Spilt blood enough to swim in:
We orphaned many children,
And widowed many women.
The eagles and the ravens
We glutted with our foemen;
The heroes and the cravens,
The spearmen and the bowmen.

We brought away from battle,
And much their land bemoaned them,
Two thousand head of cattle,
And the head of him who owned them:
Ednyfed, king of Dyfed,
His head was borne before us;
His wine and beasts supplied our feasts,
And his overthrow, our chorus.

title: The Recipe He Wrote Nine Years Before He Followed It
standfirst: In 1820 Thomas Love Peacock published an essay arguing that the earliest poems ever made were boastful war-songs about slaughter, widows and stolen land. Nine years later, inside a comic Welsh romance, he sat down and wrote one.

sections.heading: Three Trades Flourishing
sections.body:
The war-song ends on a trade: two thousand head of cattle, and the head of the man who owned them, carried before the victors like a third kind of livestock. It reads like something dug up from an old bardic collection, and it very nearly was — except that nine years before he wrote it, Thomas Love Peacock had already written down what such a thing would need to contain.

In 1820 Peacock published an essay, *The Four Ages of Poetry*, arguing that verse began not as inspiration but as advertising. Early society, he wrote, ran on "only three trades flourishing (besides that of priest which flourishes always)... those of king, thief, and beggar: the beggar being for the most part a king deject, and the thief a king expectant." Into that world stepped the bard, whose job was to record "how many battles such an one has fought, how many helmets he has cleft, how many breastplates he has pierced, how many widows he has made, how much land he has appropriated." Peacock called this the Iron Age of poetry. He did not mean it as a compliment, to himself or to anyone else currently writing verse.

sections.heading: A Reply He Never Read
sections.body:
The essay aimed past its stated subject. Peacock's real target was the poetry of his own day, which he argued had regressed toward this primitive mode rather than advanced past it — a "second childhood" dressed up as a return to nature. His closest reader took it personally. Percy Bysshe Shelley, Peacock's friend since 1812, wrote to him that "your anathemas against poetry itself excited me to a sacred rage," and spent February and March 1821 writing *A Defence of Poetry* in reply.

Shelley never finished preparing it for print, and he died the following year. The essay went unpublished until 1840, when his widow Mary Shelley brought it out eighteen years after his death — by which point Peacock, who spent much of that time as Shelley's own literary executor, had long since written and published his own answer to the question, in the shape of a war-song he presented as genuine.

sections.heading: A Castle That Never Stood, In a Kingdom That Did
sections.body:
*The Misfortunes of Elphin* (1829) sets the song at Dinas Vawr, a fortress just stormed by King Melvas, whose soldiers are celebrating with wine when the bard Taliesin arrives. Dinas Vawr — from the Welsh *fawr*, great — appears nowhere outside Peacock's own pages, and neither does the king it belongs to: no Ednyfed turns up in the surviving king-lists of Dyfed, the real and much-contested sixth-century Welsh kingdom Peacock borrowed for the setting.

The material around the invention was not invented. Peacock had walked through Wales in 1810–11, married a Welsh woman, Jane Gryffydh, in 1820, and researched the novel from early sources most of his contemporaries considered unfit for serious fiction — the *Black Book of Carmarthen*, the *Hanes Taliesin*, Owen Jones's *Myvyrian Archaiology*. The forgery is built out of real scholarship. Only the song, and the men singing it, are his.

sections.heading: Every Line Answers the Essay
sections.body:
Set the checklist from the essay against the poem and it reads like Peacock ticking his own boxes. Helmets cleft, breastplates pierced:

> We met a host, and quelled it;
> We forced a strong position,
> And killed the men who held it.

Widows made:

> We orphaned many children,
> And widowed many women.

Land appropriated, converted here into livestock and a severed head:

> Two thousand head of cattle,
> And the head of him who owned them.

Nothing here softens into metaphor. The song does not mourn the widows it makes; it counts them in the same breath as the cattle, because that is the exact transaction the essay had described nine years earlier. Peacock is not paraphrasing his own theory. He is performing it, first person plural, with precisely the swagger he said such songs would have.

sections.heading: Too Fast for Dylan Thomas
sections.body:
What the essay does not predict is how good the specimen would turn out to be. The poem has been recorded again and again since — Dylan Thomas read it for one album, Glyn Maxwell more recently for the Poetry Archive — and the critic Greg Olear has argued that most performances get it wrong by playing it stately. Of Thomas's reading he wrote: "While he certainly has a nice voice, I think his rendition, lugubrious as it is, misses the point... This is basically a rap song: less 'Danny Boy,' more 'Not Like Us.'"

That mismatch is the joke turning on itself. Readers keep trying to dignify a poem built to be undignified — the same "tumid hyperbole" *The Four Ages of Poetry* had already diagnosed, now performed for laughs rather than filed as a specimen. Peacock spent his essay arguing that songs like this belonged to the infancy of the species, unfit for a scientific age. Two centuries on, it is the poem of his that is still read aloud.
